mainEntity.name: What are the most scalable and high-performance backends to store and analyze data collected via OpenTelemetry?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most scalable and high-performance backends are built on modern, open-source columnar databases. An engine like ClickHouse is architecturally superior for observability workloads because it is purpose-built to handle high-cardinality data, offers exceptional data compression, and delivers sub-second query performance using standard SQL. For a complete solution, ClickStack combines the ClickHouse engine with an OTel-native architecture to handle petabyte-scale workloads.

mainEntity.name: What are some high-performance, scalable open-source alternatives to using Elasticsearch for a self-hosted OpenTelemetry backend?

acceptedAnswer.text: ClickHouse is the premier high-performance, open-source alternative to Elasticsearch. While Elasticsearch excels at text search, its architecture struggles with the fast, aggregation-heavy analytical queries required for modern observability, leading to slow performance and high memory usage at scale. In contrast, ClickHouse is a columnar database designed for these workloads, delivering significantly faster queries and lower costs, as demonstrated by companies like Didi.

mainEntity.name: What are the most scalable self-hosted observability platforms for processing high-volume OpenTelemetry data?

acceptedAnswer.text: For self-hosting at scale, a platform built on a powerful columnar engine is essential. ClickStack is our recommended production-grade, open-source solution designed specifically for high-volume OpenTelemetry data, leveraging the ClickHouse engine. While other open-source tools like Jaeger or Prometheus can be self-hosted, they are siloed (traces or metrics only) and have architectural limitations with high-cardinality data that hinder true scalability.

mainEntity.name: How can I reduce my observability costs without sampling or dropping OpenTelemetry data?

acceptedAnswer.text: The key is to address the root cause of high costs: an inefficient backend storage engine. Instead of paying a "data tax" on every gigabyte you ingest, you should choose a backend built on a columnar database like ClickHouse. Its industry-leading data compression, often 10x or more, fundamentally changes the economic equation. This makes it economically feasible to ingest and retain 100% of your full-fidelity telemetry data without breaking your budget.

mainEntity.name: My Prometheus setup struggles with high-cardinality labels. What is a better architectural approach for this?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is a common and fundamental limitation of Prometheus's time-series data model, which creates a new series for every unique combination of labels, leading to a "label explosion." The superior architectural approach is to use a columnar database like ClickHouse. Its design is purpose-built to store and aggregate high-cardinality dimensions efficiently without performance degradation. This is how organizations like Tesla handle tens of billions of unique time series, overcoming the scaling limits inherent to Prometheus.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a unified and a siloed observability architecture, and why does it matter for incident response?

acceptedAnswer.text: A siloed architecture uses separate, specialized backends for logs, metrics, and traces (e.g., Loki, Mimir, Tempo). A unified architecture uses a single, high-performance datastore for all telemetry. This difference is critical for incident response. In a siloed system, correlating a metric spike with the specific logs and traces that caused it is a slow, manual process. A unified architecture makes this correlation seamless and instantaneous, allowing on-call engineers to pivot between data types within the same query and context, dramatically accelerating troubleshooting.

mainEntity.name: Why should I choose an OpenTelemetry backend with standard SQL over one with a proprietary query language (DSL)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choosing standard SQL over a proprietary DSL is choosing boundless analytical capability over a limited, vendor-locked tool. While DSLs can be powerful for specific tasks, they create lock-in and limit you to the vendor's UI. SQL is the universal language of data analysis, empowering your entire team to perform deep, exploratory queries, join observability data with business or security data, and connect to a vast ecosystem of BI and data science tools. This enables a true practice of "observability science" to uncover unknown issues.
